title: Socket hygiene primer for SDK authors: lease windows, backpressure and graceful teardown
creator: Ethan Kim
description: Create a cross-language primer and code examples (Python/TypeScript/Go) that explain recommended socket/connection lifecycle settings for typical Redwood inference workloads: per-request deadlines, connection lease windows for pooling, keep-alive vs idle pruning, graceful streaming teardown, and how these interact with SDK-level retry/backoff. The deliverable is an authorable guide plus runnable snippets that can be referenced in SDK READMEs and the Console docs. This work should reduce customer misconfiguration (thundering reconnects, socket leaks) and provide consistent defaults across SDKs while documenting opt-out knobs for advanced users.
acceptance_criteria: A concise cross-SDK document (primer) available in the SDK repo docs that covers: per-request deadlines, connection lease semantics, keep-alive/idle pruning heuristics, streaming graceful shutdown patterns, and interaction with retries/backoff

Working example snippets for Python, TypeScript, and Go that demonstrate: (a) client creation with sane defaults, (b) request-level deadline vs socket-level idle/lease settings, (c) streaming lifetime management including cancel/close patterns

Integration tests or smoke scripts that validate: socket reuse under burst load, proper early timeout handling without leaking goroutines/threads, and graceful reconnect behavior when servers return transient errors
Conservative cross-SDK defaults committed to main branches and documented opt-out flags with migration notes for existing users
At least one internal review from Runtime and Observability teams recorded in comments and follow-ups addressed
technical_notes: Background: Many customer incidents stem from aggressive per-request deadlines combined with immediate connection tear-down which causes connection storms under retry. Recommended pattern is: set a per-request logical deadline slightly lower than the tuning lease window of the pool; allow a short 'linger' lease for connections to be reused; use application-level streaming cancel semantics that close the underlying stream but not the socket immediately; enable TCP keep-alive probes with a conservative interval in long-idle deployments. For streaming, prefer half-close semantics where supported (TS/Go) and ensure the SDK surface exposes a close/finish + drain API so callers can flush vs abort. Document differences: Python asyncio vs sync socket pooling; Node long-running event loop considerations; Go goroutine leak patterns and context cancellation best practices.

Prototype code snippets for each SDK demonstrating default client creation and an example streaming request with graceful shutdown
Add small smoke harness that runs a burst of streaming requests against the staging runtime to collect connection reuse metrics
Iterate defaults based on smoke test telemetry (idle prune time, lease window, keep-alive interval)
Submit PRs to each SDK repo and docs site with snippet tests and cross-links to the Console observability dashboard for telemetry
Collect reviews from Runtime, Observability, and Developer Docs; address feedback and land changes
testing_plan: Unit tests for SDK helpers that compute deadline vs lease windows (edge cases for very short deadlines)
Integration smoke: spawn 200 concurrent short-lived requests and assert connection reuse ratio > 60% under default config
Streaming teardown test: initiate streaming responses, cancel mid-stream and assert no leaked fibers/threads after 5s
Network failure simulation: induce transient RST/close and verify retry/backoff does not trigger immediate storm (max reconnect rate enforced)
Load test against staging with telemetry to capture connection churn, active sockets, and per-route latency impact
